Exact wording

English (as recorded here)
“Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.”
French
“L'attention est la forme la plus rare et la plus pure de la générosité.”

From a letter to the poet Joë Bousquet dated 13 April 1942. The archive keeps the date because the sentence has no printed source: it exists in Weil's correspondence.

Forms in circulation that differ

  • “Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.”
  • “Attention is the purest and rarest form of generosity.”
  • “Attention is the rarest form of generosity.”

Attribution notes

Frequently misfiled as coming from Gravity and Grace or from Waiting for God, which were assembled and published after Weil's death. It comes from a letter, and the correspondent matters: Weil is writing to a wounded poet about what one person owes another's suffering, so “attention” here is a demanding discipline of self-emptying, not the everyday sense of the word. It is also sometimes attributed to Simone de Beauvoir on the strength of the shared first name.

About Simone Weil

Simone Weil (1909–1943) was a French philosopher, mystic, and political activist who taught, worked in factories, and engaged labor and anti-fascist causes. A brilliant Normalienne, she sought experiential solidarity with the oppressed.

Interpretation

Weil is writing to a friend who was severely wounded, and the sentence belongs to her claim that attention is a moral capacity rather than a cognitive one. To attend is to hold another person in view without immediately converting what you see into your own purposes. She calls it rare because most apparent generosity costs the giver little attention — money, sympathy, agreement. She calls it pure because it cannot be faked for long and does not flatter the one who gives it.

Why it matters

The everyday failure is listening while preparing a reply. Weil's standard is narrower and harder: can you stay with what someone is actually saying long enough for it to change what you were about to say?

Questions readers arrive with

What is the source of the quotation “Attention is the rarest and purest form of…”?

“Attention is the rarest and purest form of…” comes from Letter to Joë Bousquet, (13 Apr 1942), attributed to Simone Weil.

What does Simone Weil mean by attention?

Across 4 recurring voices here (notably Simone Weil and Iris Murdoch), attention is framed through Religious Existentialism and Platonic Moral Philosophy. Some passages define attention; others warn how it fails; still others relocate it inside habit, community, or language. This passage enters that discussion through attention, love.

Is the wording of this Simone Weil quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.” Forms in circulation that differ: Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. / Attention is the purest and rarest form of generosity. / Attention is the rarest form of generosity. The French reads “L'attention est la forme la plus rare et la plus pure de la générosité.”

Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Frequently misfiled as coming from Gravity and Grace or from Waiting for God, which were assembled and published after Weil's death. It comes from a letter, and the correspondent matters: Weil is writing to a wounded poet about what one person owes another's suffering, so “attention” here is a demanding discipline of self-emptying, not the everyday sense of the word. It is also sometimes attributed to Simone de Beauvoir on the strength of the shared first name.
